questions.question: What is an Angular component, and how does its template connect to the class?
questions.title: Angular Components and Templates
questions.direct_answer: An Angular component is a TypeScript class marked with `@Component` metadata. The metadata gives it a selector and template, while the template reads public class members through bindings and calls class methods through event listeners.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `@Component` marks a class as an Angular component.
The selector identifies where the component appears in another template.
The template reads class values with expressions and bindings.
Event bindings call class methods when the user interacts.
Component imports make child components, directives, and pipes available locally.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
An Angular component is the unit that owns one part of the user interface. It is a TypeScript class with `@Component` metadata. The metadata supplies a selector, a template or template URL, optional styles, and the imports needed by that template. Angular creates an instance of the class whenever the component is rendered.

The class-to-template connection is made through binding. Interpolation can read a field such as `{{ productName }}`. A property binding can pass a class value to an element or child component. An event binding can call a class method. The template is compiled, so Angular can check whether referenced members and child components exist.

For example, a product card can store `name` and `inStock` in its class. Its template displays the name and disables a Buy button when the item is unavailable. A click event calls `buy()` on that same card instance.

A component should have a clear visual responsibility. Putting API calls, business rules, and unrelated page state into every component makes the class hard to test and reuse; shared work often belongs in a service. The template should also avoid expensive calculations because expressions may run during checks. In short, the class owns state and actions, metadata defines the component boundary, and the compiled template turns that state into a view.

sections.title: One component instance and one owned view
sections.content:
The selector is the component's HTML name. If the selector is `product-card`, a parent can place `<product-card />` in its template after importing that component. Angular does not copy the child class into the parent; it creates a separate child instance with its own state and view.

Inside the child's template, expressions run in the context of that child instance. A reference to `name` means `this.name` conceptually, although templates do not write `this` in most cases. Events cross the other direction: a browser click is handled by the listener declared in the template, which calls a class method and may change state.

Metadata completes the boundary. `imports` exposes template dependencies, while styles normally apply to the component view according to its encapsulation mode. Inputs and outputs can make selected values and events public to a parent without exposing all class details.

The class is not a replacement for semantic HTML. A card should still use headings, buttons, and links with their normal meanings. Angular manages creation and binding, while the browser manages the resulting accessible elements. A focused component combines both: a small stateful class and a template that clearly describes the view.

sections.title: The component boundary
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Parent[Parent template] -->|selector and inputs| Meta[Component metadata]
  Meta --> Class[Component class]
  Class -->|values and methods| Template[Compiled template]
  Template --> DOM[Owned DOM view]
  DOM -->|browser events| Template
  Template -->|method call| Class
```

questions.question: What are interpolation, property binding, event binding, and two-way binding in Angular?
questions.title: Angular Template Binding Forms
questions.direct_answer: Interpolation renders text, property binding writes a value to a DOM, directive, or component property, event binding listens for an event, and two-way binding combines an input and matching change event so data can move in both directions.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `{{ value }}` converts a value to text in the rendered view.
`[property]="expression" writes the evaluated value to a property.
`(event)="handler($event)" runs code when an event occurs.
`[(ngModel)]` combines a value binding and change listener for form controls.
Attribute bindings use `[attr.name]` when an HTML attribute is required.

sections.title: Interview answer
Binding direction and browser properties
sections.content:
Interpolation and property binding both read an Angular expression, but they target different things. Interpolation produces text. Property binding assigns a value to a property such as `HTMLButtonElement.disabled` or to an input on a child component. When a true HTML attribute is required, such as `aria-label` or a table span, the `attr.` form targets the attribute explicitly.

Event binding creates the return path. A click, input, or custom component output carries an event to the class. The handler can update ordinary state or a signal, which then gives Angular a reason to refresh the affected binding. Angular expressions are intentionally narrower than arbitrary JavaScript and should remain short and predictable.

Two-way binding is syntax for a paired input and output. `[(ngModel)]` sets the control from a component value and writes user changes back to that value. A component model input similarly exposes a value and a matching `Change` output. It is not a separate transport system; it is a compact contract between two existing directions.

Do not use string attributes where a live property is required. `disabled="false"` still places the Boolean attribute on a native button, while `[disabled]="false"` sets the property to false. Understanding the target prevents many template bugs.

sections.title: Binding syntax and data direction
sections.content:
| Syntax | Direction | Target | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `{{ value }}` | class → text | text node | labels and messages |
| `[prop]="value"` | class → property | DOM, directive, or component | disabled state or child input |
| `(event)="action()"` | event → class | listener | click or custom output |
| `[(ngModel)]="value"` | both directions | form control | editable field |

questions.question: How do parent and child Angular components communicate with inputs and outputs?
questions.title: Component Inputs and Outputs
questions.direct_answer: A child exposes inputs for values received from its parent and outputs for events sent back. The parent uses property binding to supply an input and event binding to handle an output, which keeps data ownership explicit.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: An input is a public value that a parent can bind into a child.
An output is a custom event that a child can emit to its parent.
Modern Angular uses `input()` and `output()` for typed component contracts.
Custom Angular outputs do not bubble through the DOM.
Keep the owning state in the parent and emit user intent from the child.

sections.title: Interview answer
Data ownership across a component boundary
sections.content:
A parent template can bind an expression to a child's input. Angular evaluates that expression in the parent context and supplies the result to the child. With an input signal, the child calls the signal in its class or template. Required inputs are checked by the compiler when the child is used in a template that Angular can analyse.

The child should report actions rather than reach into its parent. A `selected` output can carry a user ID, while the parent decides whether to open details, update a route, or ignore the action. This keeps the child reusable. Output names should describe what happened, not command the parent to call a particular method.

Suppose a list owns an array of users. It passes one user into each card. When a card button is clicked, the card emits that user's ID. The list receives the event and stores the selected ID. The input and output form a loop at the application level, but each direction remains explicit at the component boundary.

Inputs are not automatically immutable. TypeScript's `readonly` and careful update patterns can express that intent. Also avoid naming custom outputs after native DOM events, because a parent reader may not know which source produced the event. Use a service only when communication is genuinely shared beyond a clear parent-child relationship.

sections.title: Parent-child data and event flow
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  State[Parent-owned state] -->|property binding| Input[Child input]
  Input --> View[Child view]
  View -->|user action| Output[Child output]
  Output -->|event binding| Handler[Parent handler]
  Handler --> State
```
